Class IuRefreshableCache<K,V>

java.lang.Object
edu.iu.IuRefreshableCache<K,V>
Type Parameters:
K - cache key type
V - cached value type
All Implemented Interfaces:
UnsafeFunction<K,V>, AutoCloseable
public class IuRefreshableCache<K,V> extends Object implements UnsafeFunction<K,V>, AutoCloseable
A refresh-ahead cache for values resolved by an UnsafeFunction, with hint-directed caching, background refresh, downstream outage tolerance, and deferred invalidation.

This cache is a defensive short-term cache: it exists to keep an actively read value close at hand and to absorb a brief downstream outage, not to serve as a system of record. It is designed for values that are read far more often than they change, resolved from a stable backing source, and tolerable to serve slightly stale.

Lookup lifecycle

Every apply(Object) invocation proceeds through the same steps.

  1. Hint: the cache hint function is consulted for the key. A null hint bypasses the cache entirely for that invocation.
  2. Configuration snapshot: the configuration supplier is read and its values validated. An invalid value fails this invocation only; the cache itself is left intact.
  3. Call pool: the thread pool is resolved, and replaced if its size no longer matches the configuration.
  4. Cache decision: the invocation either bypasses the cache (see Uncached invocations) or resolves against it (see Cached invocations).

Uncached invocations

An invocation bypasses the cache when caching is disabled (refresh TTL is null), the hint function returned null, or the hint's shouldClear returns true for its own key. The last case is the write key idiom: a key that mutates the backing source is never itself cached, and on success publishes an invalidation for the keys it affected.

An uncached call is dispatched to the pool and joined in line, bounded by the call TTL; on timeout the call is cancelled, since no other caller is waiting on it. Invalidation is published only after the call succeeds, so a failed write never discards good cached data.

Cached invocations

A cached invocation resolves to exactly one of four outcomes.

hit
The entry holds a value published less than one refresh TTL ago. It is returned without any call.
hit, refreshing
The entry holds a value older than the refresh TTL. The caller returns that value immediately and a refresh runs in the background. This is the common steady-state path: readers never pay for a refresh.
miss
The entry holds no value — it was never populated, it was invalidated, or the cache TTL elapsed without a successful refresh. The caller waits, bounded by the call TTL. All concurrent callers for the same key share one invocation and one result — or one failure. On timeout the call is left running, so it can still populate the cache for the callers behind it.
degraded
A refresh failed, or could not be dispatched because the pending queue was full. The last good value continues to be served, at INFO, until the cache TTL elapses. Only once there is no last good value does a caller see the failure.

Time to live

Three independent intervals govern an entry, measured from the moment its last successful refresh was published.

refresh TTL
How long a value is served without triggering a refresh. This is the staleness bound under healthy conditions. Null disables caching entirely, and the cache TTL is then unused.
cache TTL
How long a value remains available once refreshes stop succeeding; must be longer than the refresh TTL. The interval between the two is the outage tolerance window. A successful refresh restarts the window, so a healthy entry never expires.
call TTL
How long any single call may run. It also bounds a background refresh: a refresh still in flight after the call TTL is cancelled and replaced, so a hung call cannot block every later refresh for its key.

Publication time is stored rather than a derived expiration, so a reconfigured refresh TTL applies immediately to entries already cached, in both directions, without discarding them. The cache TTL is applied as each entry is stored, so a reconfigured cache TTL takes effect for an entry at its next successful refresh.

Cache hints

The hint function supplied at construction is consulted once per invocation, before the cache is read, so it should be inexpensive: its cost is paid on every cache hit. The IuRefreshableCacheHint it returns directs three separate behaviors.

IuRefreshableCacheHint.shouldClear(Object)
Serves a dual role. Evaluated against the invocation's own key it selects the uncached write-key path described above. Evaluated against other keys, after that call succeeds, it selects which cached entries the write invalidated.
IuRefreshableCacheHint.restore()
Supplies a value resolved elsewhere — typically by a peer node in the same cluster — in place of calling the refresh function. It is consulted at the start of every refresh, including the first, so a hint that always restores never contacts the backing source at all. It is not consulted on the uncached path.
IuRefreshableCacheHint.inspect(Object)
Extracts related values embedded in a result and publishes them under their own keys, so a single call can populate many entries. Because a restored value short-circuits the refresh function, inspection is skipped for restored values.

Invalidation

Invalidation is deferred rather than applied eagerly, because a hint describes which keys it affects by predicate rather than by enumeration.

IuRefreshableCacheHint.clearAll() is the exception: it is recognized by identity, and immediately after a successful call it discards every pending invalidation and then clears the entire cache, both in line. A hint that merely returns true from shouldClear for every key is not equivalent — it takes the deferred path below.

Every other invalidating hint is queued, timestamped at the moment its call succeeded. Each cached lookup then scans that queue, under the entry's own monitor, and applies three rules to each event in turn.

purge
An event older than the cache TTL is ejected from the queue. Nothing it could still match has survived that long, so this is housekeeping: it bounds queue growth, and does not affect any result.
skip
An event that precedes the entry's own position in the invalidation sequence is ignored for that entry, because the value on hand was published after it. Ordering is by sequence rather than by timestamp, so two events that fall in the same clock tick are still ordered, and an invalidation can never tie with a publication and be lost. The event remains queued for other entries.
clear
Otherwise the event's shouldClear is consulted for the key. On the first match the entry's value is discarded and the scan stops, converting the lookup into a miss; a refresh already in flight for that key is abandoned, since it too predates the invalidation. The matching event is not removed: it stays queued for other entries, but stops matching this one, whose replacement takes a later position in the sequence.

An invalidation therefore costs one refresh per affected key, not one per subsequent read.

Implementation Note: apart from a clear-all and close(), which drain it outright, the queue is drained only by cached lookups, and the scan stops at the first matching event. A workload with no cached reads, or one whose reads match early in the queue, does not purge. Scan cost is proportional to queue depth, which is bounded by the invalidating call rate multiplied by the cache TTL — so a long cache TTL combined with a high write rate is the configuration to avoid. shouldClear is invoked while the entry monitor is held, so it must return quickly and must not invoke a remote method or touch this cache.

Call pool

All calls, foreground and background alike, run on a lazily created pool of daemon threads sized by threads with a bounded backlog of pending calls. Idle threads time out, so an idle cache holds no threads. Changing either value replaces the pool; the replaced pool is shut down gracefully so calls already in flight run to completion.

A full backlog rejects the dispatch. For a key with a last good value that is absorbed — the stale value is served — so the pool bounds are a load-shedding control, not only a resource control. Sizing them too tightly converts pressure into staleness; sizing them too loosely converts it into latency.

Because calls run on pooled threads, thread-bound context does not reach them unless forwarded. See captureContext(), which forwards the context ClassLoader and may be overridden to forward more.

Tuning

read latency
Governed by the refresh TTL. Short enough to keep values current, long enough that most reads are hits.
staleness
Bounded by the refresh TTL while healthy, and by the cache TTL while degraded.
outage tolerance
The cache TTL less the refresh TTL. Widen to survive a longer downstream outage; narrow to fail faster on one.
downstream load
Roughly one call per key per refresh TTL, plus one per uncached invocation. Lengthen the refresh TTL to reduce it; use IuRefreshableCacheHint.inspect(Object) to populate many keys per call.
invalidation scan cost
Proportional to cache TTL times the invalidating call rate. Reduce by shortening the cache TTL, or by making invalidation coarse (clear-all) instead of predicate-based.
concurrency and backpressure
Threads and pending, as described above.
failure latency
The call TTL, which is also the ceiling on how long a hung refresh occupies a pool thread before it is cancelled.

Sound starting points: a refresh TTL of minutes, a cache TTL no longer than PT30M, and a call TTL short enough that a stalled downstream is noticed promptly. See IuRefreshableCacheConfiguration for defaults.

Concurrency and lifecycle

This class is thread-safe. Concurrent first callers for one key share a single entry and a single invocation. Each entry's mutable state is guarded by its own monitor, so lookups of distinct keys do not contend on it.

The cache is shared by all callers regardless of the context they call from. When forwarded context can change a result, fold the distinguishing context into the cache key; otherwise a result resolved in one context is served in another.

The configuration supplier is read on every invocation, so an application may reconfigure TTLs and pool limits in place without replacing the cache. Instances own a lazily created executor and must be closed when no longer needed; close() is idempotent and further invocations fail with IllegalStateException.

    • IuRefreshableCache

      public IuRefreshableCache(Supplier<IuRefreshableCacheConfiguration> config, UnsafeFunction<K,V> refreshFunction, Function<K, IuRefreshableCacheHint<K,V>> cacheHintFunction)
      Creates a refresh-ahead cache with a dynamically supplied configuration and a policy for keys eligible for caching.

      Both functions are consulted once per invocation, so returning current values allows the cache to be reconfigured in place. See IuRefreshableCache for how each configured value takes effect, and for a description of the defensive call cache, which is enabled when IuRefreshableCacheConfiguration.getRefreshTtl() is non-null.

      Configured values are validated when observed rather than here, so an invalid configuration fails the invocation that reads it, not construction.

      Parameters:
      config - supplies the configuration in effect; should return quickly, as it is called on every invocation
      refreshFunction - function that resolves cached values on a cache miss and on each background refresh; invoked on a pooled thread
      cacheHintFunction - function that directs how a key interacts with the cache; should return quickly, as it is called on every invocation before the cache is read. A null function, or one that returns null for a key, bypasses the cache for that key

  • Method Details

    • captureContext

      protected Supplier<Runnable> captureContext()
      Captures the calling thread's context for forwarding to the asynchronous call.

      Since every remote call runs on a pooled thread, thread-bound context does not reach it unless it is forwarded. This method drives that in three phases.

      1. Capture: this method is invoked on the calling thread, and reads whatever context is to be forwarded.
      2. Apply: the returned Supplier is invoked on the pooled thread immediately before the call, and returns a Runnable that undoes it.
      3. Restore: that Runnable is invoked on the pooled thread after the call completes, whether or not it succeeded. The pool is shared, so a call must leave the thread as it found it.

      Default behavior is to forward the context ClassLoader and nothing else. In particular, no other ThreadLocal-bound state reaches the call. Subclasses may override to forward additional context, e.g. a security principal or a diagnostic context; such an override should delegate to super.captureContext() so the context ClassLoader continues to be forwarded.

      Because a stale entry is refreshed in the background, a refresh runs under the context captured from whichever caller happened to trigger it, and its result is then served to every caller. The cache is internal and shared by all contexts, so when forwarded context can change the result, override to fold the distinguishing context into the cache key; otherwise a result from one context is served to another.

      Implementation Note: capture runs on the calling thread while a lock on the cache entry is held, so it should return quickly and must not invoke a remote method. An apply phase that fails should leave the thread unmodified, since its restore Runnable is never invoked. A failed restore is propagated after a successful call; when the call also fails, the restore failure is suppressed on that call failure.

      Returns:
      Supplier that applies the captured context to the pooled thread and returns a Runnable that restores it

    • mark

      public long mark()
      Reads this cache's current position in the invalidation sequence, for publishing a value that is about to be read from the backing source.

      Take a mark before reading the value it will be published with, so that an invalidation raised while that read is in progress is newer than the value and correctly discards it. Taking it afterward would stamp the value as though it had observed a change it could not have seen.

      The one case that wants the opposite order is a caller republishing a value it has just written: take the mark after the invalidation describing that write, so the replacement outranks it rather than being discarded by it.

      Returns:
      opaque sequence position, for publish(Object, Object, long)
      See Also:
      • publish(Object, Object, long)

    • publish

      public boolean publish(K key, V value, long mark)
      Publishes a value obtained outside this cache, as though the cache had resolved it itself.

      Intended for a caller that has already paid for a value the cache would otherwise have to fetch — a read performed for another purpose, or the state a write just established — so that the next reader is served without a call.

      The value is published as though read at mark, so every invalidation raised since then still applies to it. It is declined, and this method returns false, when an invalidation newer than mark matches key, or when the entry already holds a value read more recently. A declined value is simply not published; nothing else about the entry changes.

      Publishing supersedes a refresh already in flight for key. Under a refresh TTL short enough for the load the cache is carrying, a value lost that way is re-read within one refresh interval.

      Parameters:
      key - cache key
      value - value to publish; may be null, which publishes a cached null
      mark - sequence position from mark(), read before the value
      Returns:
      true if the value was published; false if it was declined as stale, or if caching is disabled by the configuration in effect
      Throws:
      IllegalStateException - if this cache has been closed
      See Also:
      • mark()

    • close

      public void close()
      Releases the thread pool backing this cache, and discards all cached results and all pending invalidations.

      In-flight calls are interrupted. Once closed, further invocations fail with IllegalStateException. This method is idempotent.
